title: Leading Team Members Who Start Out Strong But Fizzle Out Over Time
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership piece examines one of the most frustrating patterns in people management: the team member who starts powerfully — strong results, cultural fit, apparent confidence — and then, over one to three years, loses momentum and begins to underperform. The article outlines the most common explanations for this arc, beginning with role-person mismatch as the person grows but the role stays static, and the disengagement that follows when ambition outpaces opportunity. A second explanation is relational: the team member's confidence in leadership, the mission, or the culture erodes — what the article calls 'disillusionment as a quiet saboteur.' The article also identifies performance anxiety (fear of falling short of the high standard set early), external life changes that shift priorities, and—most difficult—chronic overextension where the early strong results came at an unsustainable personal cost. The most important practical implication is the leader's first task: generating a thoughtful theory of why, which requires the leader to actually ask the team member rather than guessing.
points: Role-person mismatch over time is the most common and most correctable explanation: people grow, and when their evolution outpaces the role's scope, disengagement is almost inevitable — a modest adjustment to responsibilities often reignites the original energy.

Disillusionment — eroded confidence in leadership, mission, or culture — is 'a quiet saboteur': it rarely announces itself, makes strong early performers appear inexplicably diminished, and requires direct exploratory conversation to surface.

Performance anxiety is a counterintuitive risk for initially strong performers: the high standard they set early creates an implicit pressure to maintain it, and the fear of falling short sometimes produces the very underperformance it fears.

The leader's most important first move is generating a theory of why rather than reacting to the underperformance — and generating a theory requires asking the team member directly, which most leaders avoid because the conversation is uncomfortable.

Not all performance fade is fixable: some causes are unchangeable (life priorities have genuinely shifted, the person has found better work elsewhere), and the leader's role in those cases is to help the person exit well rather than to engineer a recovery that won't last.
quotes: Team members who start out strong, demonstrate their skills through results, and appear to settle comfortably into the culture are a big win for leaders. But over time, these capable people sometimes lose their momentum, begin to underperform, and seem very different from the persona they projected early on.

Leading team members who begin powerfully but fizzle out over time is both highly disappointing and a unique challenge for leaders. There are many reasons a team member’s performance can drop off a cliff after a couple of years of strong results — some preventable, others coachable, and a few that may well be unchangeable.
The first task of the leader is to generate a theory as to why. Exploring this reality, no matter how uncomfortable it might be for both parties, is the place to start formulating an explanation.

Among the most common explanations for this performance arc is a mismatch between the role and the person’s evolving ambitions. People grow, and what once excited and challenged the team member may no longer hold the same appeal.

When the role remains static even as the person develops new interests, stronger skills, or broader aspirations, disengagement becomes almost inevitable. Leaders who surface this possibility early often discover that a modest adjustment in responsibilities, scope, or opportunity is all that is needed to reignite the energy and output that once defined the team member’s contribution.

A second and more difficult explanation involves the team member’s relationship with the organization itself. Sometimes what fizzles is not the person’s competence but their confidence in leadership, their belief in the mission, or their trust in the culture they once embraced.

It is rarely announced and easily mistaken for laziness or indifference. Sometimes the disengagement can be rectified by exploring why they have come to believe what they do and advocating for a different frame or interpretation of the events and incidents that created their distrust.
